name: Decolonization
summary: Decolonization is the political programme of ending colonial rule and undoing its legacies. Its core demands are the right of colonized peoples to self-determination and independence without delay, the end of colonial exploitation and racial discrimination, and control of national resources. The Fanonist strand adds that independence is empty without an economic and social transformation led by the masses, and that the colonized should not copy European institutions. Indigenous and decolonial-turn scholarship extend the term to settler colonialism, land return and knowledge.
scope: The anti-colonial programme as set out in the UN Declaration on granting independence to colonial peoples (Resolution 1514, 1960) and in Frantz Fanon's The Wretched of the Earth, the thinker the reference entries name as its revolutionary theorist (s8), together with Ngugi wa Thiong'o on cultural and linguistic decolonization (s8, s6) and the scholarship that extends the term to settler colonialism (Tuck and Yang) and to knowledge (Maldonado-Torres). Where these sources are silent on a question the answer is null; Fanon's 'Concerning Violence' chapter could not be opened from an official copy, so his views on violence rest on the encyclopedia entry's report (s8). It does not cover colonialism itself, the later policies of any decolonizing empire (s9 treats British devolution of power), or other anti-imperialisms.

notes: Themes searched: self-determination and independence (UN 1514), economy and property after independence, party and state form, nationalization, land, ethnic nationalism and expulsion, culture and language, Indigenous land and settler colonialism, violence. Government, world, ecology, technology, gender, religion and many liberty and means themes are not addressed by the sources, so most answers are null and the uncertainty rule is expected to fail. Fanon's 'Concerning Violence' chapter and the Bandung communique were not obtainable from official open copies (a bot check on the latter), so neither is cited; violence answers rest on the reference entry's report of Fanon.
